title: Successful neoadjuvant treatment of EGFR exon 19 deletion combined with TP53 mutation in non-small cell lung cancer using aumolertinib after osimertinib-induced myocardial damage: a case report and literature review
author: Guijuan Zhang; Xiaoyuan Tang; Xingping Zhang; Xingting Qiu; Qingwen Lai; Jie Li
text:
Abstract
The development of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) represents a paradigm shift in the treatment of lung cancer with EGFR mutations. Aumolertinib has been shown to be a safe agent in the registry study. However, successful rechallenge with aumolertinib following osimertinib-induced myocardial damage has not been reported. In this article, a case of neoadjuvant therapy for lung adenocarcinoma is retrospectively analyzed, and the relevant literature is reviewed. The patient was diagnosed with stage IIIA lung adenocarcinoma, and genetic testing revealed EGFR exon 19 deletion mutation combined with Tumor Protein p53 (TP53) mutation. The mutation abundance is 33.5 and 14%, respectively. One month after osimertinib treatment, the patient developed myocardial damage, and abnormal indicators such as myocardial enzyme spectrum showed abnormalities and cardiac insufficiency, followed by pulmonary hypertension and pulmonary edema. Aumolertinib was subsequently used for treatment, following which the myocardial enzyme spectrum returned to normal, and the symptoms of bilateral interstitial edema disappeared. In addition to the disappearance of adverse reactions, the therapeutic effect was excellent; the lung lesions and mediastinal lymph nodes were significantly reduced, and the operation was successfully conducted. This is the first report of successful neoadjuvant treatment of EGFR exon 19 deletion combined with TP53 mutation in NSCLC using aumolertinib after osimertinib-induced myocardial damage. The results suggested that aumolertinib had fewer adverse reactions in patients with EGFR exon 19 deletion combined with TP53 mutation, and aumolertinib may be a potential neoadjuvant therapy for stage IIIA lung cancer.
Keywords: aumolertinib, case report, epidermal growth factor receptor, osimertinib
Introduction
Lung cancer is one of the most serious malignant tumors in the world. GLOBOCAN estimates that in 2020, there will be approximately 2.2 million new cases of lung cancer worldwide, accounting for 11.4% of all malignancies, and approximately 1.8 million deaths, accounting for 18.0% of malignant tumor-related deaths [1]. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most common type of lung cancer, accounting for approximately 85% of all lung cancers, with a 5-year survival rate of less than 15% [2,3]. Patients with advanced NSCLC with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutation form a special group, which is sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) of EGFR and shows significantly improved progression-free survival and objective response rate [4]. Several clinical studies have confirmed that first-generation EGFR-TKIs (gefitinib [5], erlotinib [6], and icotinib [7]) and second-generation EGFR-TKIs (afatinib [8] and dacomitinib [9]) used in the first-line treatment compared with platinum-based chemotherapy have clinical benefits in advanced NSCLC with EGFR mutation. Most patients treated with first and second-generation EGFR TKIs relapse and develop resistance to treatment; EGFR T790M is the most common mutation that causes drug resistance, aumolertinib is an oral third-generation irreversible EGFR-TKI for EGFR T790M mutation NSCLC [10], which is currently recommended in patients who had an initial response to first-generation EGFR-TKI treatment and had subsequent disease progression. A double-blinded phase 3 randomized control trial compared the effectiveness of standard TKIs, including gefitinib and aumolertinib. The study showed that aumolertinib had superior efficacy to gefitinib in first-line treatment of EGFR mutation-positive NSCLC, and the adverse reactions were well tolerated and controllable [11].
However, the adverse reactions of the third-generation EGFR TKI, especially cardiac toxicity, have drawn attention. According to clinical data, the incidence of adverse reactions between osimertinib and aumolertinib treatment is differentiated. Whether we can switch to aumolertinib treatment when osimertinib has adverse reactions leading to drug withdrawal is an urgent issue to be explored. We reported a case of an NSCLC patient who developed cardiotoxicity after neoadjuvant therapy with osimertinib. After symptomatic treatment and recovery, aumolertinib was administered with no adverse reactions, and surgery was performed successfully.
Case presentation
A 69-year-old woman was admitted to the first affiliated hospital of Gannan Medical University on 5 May 2021 due to complaints of dyspnea for 6 months and cough for half a month. Computed tomography (CT) imaging revealed a space-occupying lesion in the middle lobe of the right lung, which suggested the possibility of peripheral lung cancer (Fig. 1a). CT-guided needle biopsy of the lung lesion was thus performed to confirm the diagnosis. Pathological finding: (right lung biopsy) adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemical assay: S2110434-A03#: CK(+), NapsinA(+), TTF-1(+), Ki-67 (around 20%+), ALK(D5F3)(−), P40(−), CgA(−), and CD56(−). Genetic testing was performed using paraffin sections of biopsy tissue, which revealed mutations of EGFR in exon 19 and mutations of the Tumor Protein TP53 (TP53) gene, gene mutation analysis using sequence capture and high-throughput sequencing; PD-L1 immunohistochemistry: TPS around 90%. On the basis of the discussions of multi-disciplinary treatment (MDT) at the hospital, it was concluded that the patient had a clinical stage of T2bN2M0 IIIA and indications for surgery. However, given that the patient had multiple enlarged hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes abutting the upper and lower lobes, it was recommended that the patient undergoes two courses of preoperative neoadjuvant chemotherapy or preoperative targeted therapy and waits until shrinkage of primary tumor masses and enlarged lymph nodes before receiving surgical treatment. This patient was eventually diagnosed with a malignant neoplasm of the right middle lobe featuring EGFR mutations in exon 19 and TP53 mutations (stage T2bN2M0 IIIA adenocarcinoma) and secondary malignant neoplasm of intrathoracic lymph nodes. On 17 May 2021, treatment with third-generation EGFR-TKI osimertinib (80 mg daily) was initiated. The patient started to develop paroxysmal dry cough with dyspnea on 10 June 2021; on 15 June 2021, the patient returned to the hospital for re-examination, and the post-admission physical lung examination revealed ‘Velcro-type’ crackles in both lower lobes on chest auscultation. A chest CT re-examination was subsequently performed for comparison with the CT findings on 6 May 2021. The CT scan results showed reduced size of the tumor masses and slightly larger multiple enlarged mediastinal and right hilar lymph nodes compared with those previously examined. New findings included infection and interstitial changes in both lungs and bilateral pleural effusion, as well as multiple nodules and multiple fibrotic lesions in both lungs (Fig. 1b). Color Doppler echocardiography suggested: (1) left atrial enlargement; (2) aortic valve regurgitation (mild); mitral valve regurgitation (mild); tricuspid valve regurgitation (mild+); (3) slightly enlarged pulmonary arteries indicating pulmonary arterial hypertension; and (4) left ventricular diastolic dysfunction and systolic function within the normal range. The myocardial enzyme profile revealed by routine re-examination on 15 June 2021: lactate dehydrogenase (rate assay) 345 U/L, α-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase 292 U/L, and creatine phosphokinase 648 U/L. Quantitative fluorescence analysis suggested troponin I <0.01 ng/mL, myohemoglobin 44 ng/mL, and N-terminal brain natriuretic peptide precursor 2015 pg/mL. The level of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was 5.76 ng/mL (the level of CEA was detected at 37.3 ng/mL on 5 May 2021). Examination of the pleural effusion and the pericardial effusion showed a small amount of pleural effusion on both sides and an absence of effusion in the pericardial cavity. On 16 June 2021, B-ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration on the right side was performed on the patient. Routine and biochemical assays for the aspirated pleural effusion were subsequently conducted, suggesting the transudative nature of the pleural fluid. A cytology exam of pleural fluid was also performed to detect cancer cells, revealing a relatively large number of mesothelial cells, neutrophils, and macrophages, as well as a small amount of lymphocytes. No other medications were taken while the patient was taking osimertinib. After a second discussion at the MDT meeting, it was considered that the patient had an elevated CK level and possibly developed myocardial damage after oral administration of targeted drugs, which might have caused cardiac insufficiency, resulting in pulmonary arterial hypertension and pulmonary edema. The possibility of malignant pleural effusion was ruled out and cardiac insufficiency and hypoproteinemia were considered the causes of pleural effusion. Suspension of osimertinib treatment was thus recommended, combined with the administration of levofloxacin to treat infections, administration of trimetazidine + vitamin C to nourish the myocardium, correction of hypoproteinemia, and the use of diuretics to reduce the cardiac workload. After 5 days of treatment, the patient experienced marked improvement in cough and dyspnea and the physical lung examination revealed that the ‘Velcro-type’ crackles in both lower lobes disappeared. Blood cell re-analysis on 19 June 2021 showed no significant abnormalities; liver function, renal function, electrolytes, myocardial enzyme profile, C-reactive protein: aspartate aminotransferase 10 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 45 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase (rate assay) 264 U/L, α-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase 202 U/L, creatine phosphokinase 50 U/L, creatine kinase isoenzyme 6 U/L, urea 2.3 mmol/L; N-terminal brain natriuretic peptide precursor test and two-item cardiac function test: myohemoglobin (chemiluminescence detection) 24 ng/mL and N-terminal brain natriuretic peptide precursor (chemiluminescence detection) 677 pg/mL. Another chest CT re-examination was performed on 20 June 2021 for comparison with the CT findings on 15 June 2021: (1) cancerous changes in the middle lobe of the right lung covering smaller areas than that observed in the previous report and multiple enlarged mediastinal and right hilar lymph nodes similar to those previously examined in the follow-up visit; (2) improved infection in both lungs compared with the previous visit; interstitial changes in both lungs; a small amount of pleural effusion on both sides less compared with the previous visit; (3) multiple nodules and multiple fibrotic lesions in both lungs; and (4) a small amount of pericardial effusion. Given the patient’s improved clinical symptoms, markedly absorbed interstitial changes in both lungs, recovery of creatine phosphokinase activity, and remarkable decrease in the level of N-terminal brain natriuretic peptide precursor, it was recommended that the patient continued to receive lung cancer therapy such as chemotherapy, direct surgery, or administration of other EGFR-TKIs (preferred choice: aumolertinib). Like other EGFR TKIs, aumolertinib also incurs the risk of inducing elevated CK levels, but previous clinical data suggested no obvious clinical symptoms in most patients; the patient subsequently chose orally administered targeted drugs for further treatment. After being discharged from the hospital on 20 June 2021 following improved conditions, the patient received oral aumolertinib (110 mg daily) for anti-tumor therapy. On 17 July 2021, the patient returned to the hospital for re-examination which revealed lactate dehydrogenase (rate assay) at 235 U/L, creatine phosphokinase at 227 U/L, N-terminal brain natriuretic peptide precursor (fluorescence quantification) at 92.4 pg/mL, and CEA at 3.79 ng/mL (CEA at 37.3 ng/mL on 5 May 2021 and CEA at 5.76 ng/mL on 15 June 2021); contrast-enhanced chest CT scan was performed on 17 July 2021 for comparison with the CT findings on 20 June 2021, with the following findings: lesions in the right middle lobe satisfying the criteria for cancerous changes to the lung; multiple enlarged mediastinal and right hilar lymph nodes similar to those previously examined in the follow-up visit; mild and improved infection in both lungs compared with the previous visit; absorption of previous interstitial edema in both lungs; the small amount of previous pleural effusion on both sides basically absorbed; multiple nodules and multiple fibrotic lesions in both lungs as in the previous visit (Fig. 1c). Plain + contrast-enhanced brain MRI scans performed on 19 July 2021 (Fig. 2a) revealed: subdural hematoma over the left temporal and occipital lobes; thickening and enhancement of the meninges in the left temporal and occipital lobes (unconfirmed metastasis awaiting confirmation; re-examinations were recommended); abnormal signals below the left frontal cortex with no obvious changes from the MR findings on 7 May 2021, which suggested the possibility of focal encephalomalacia. At this point, the patient’s clinical symptoms had improved. A chest CT re-examination suggested improvement of the lesions, but the occurrence of newly developed brain metastases remained unconfirmed. However, the patient refused the recommended lumbar puncture or PET-CT examination and continued to receive treatment with oral aumolertinib. Follow-up examinations were performed on 4 October 2021. No abnormalities were observed in blood cell analysis, lung cancer screening, the N-terminal brain natriuretic peptide precursor test, the two-item cardiac function test, urine analysis, routine stool examination, the liver function/renal function tests, the myocardial enzyme profile, the two-item blood glucose test and the level of electrolytes, serum lipid, and C-reactive protein. Routine ECG testing revealed sinus arrhythmias and T-wave changes. A CT examination was performed on 5 October 2021 for comparison with the chest CT findings on 17 July 2021 and the whole-abdomen CT findings on 19 July 2021. The results revealed: (1) lesions in the middle lobe of the right lung covering smaller areas than those previously examined; multiple enlarged mediastinal and right hilar lymph nodes slightly smaller in size than those previously examined; (2) mild and improved infection in both lungs compared with the previous visit; and (3) multiple nodules and multiple fibrotic lesions in both lungs as in the previous visit (Fig. 1d). Plain + contrast-enhanced brain MRI scans were performed on 6 October 2021 for comparison with MR findings on 19 July 2021, and the results suggested: (1) absorption of subdural hematoma over the left temporal and occipital lobes compared with the previous visit; thickening and enhancement of the meninges in the left temporal and occipital lobes covering smaller areas compared with the previous visit (a re-examination was recommended) and (2) abnormal signals below the left frontal cortex with no obvious changes from the previous visit, which suggested the possibility of focal encephalomalacia (Fig. 2b). After evaluation by two senior radiologists, a low possibility of brain metastases was clinically considered. After consultations at the department of thoracic surgery, the patient was considered to have indications for surgery, and subsequently underwent thoracoscopic radical resection of lung cancer in the right middle lobe + lymph node dissection + cautery division of pleural adhesions on 20 October 2021. Postoperative pathological findings: (the middle lobe of the right lung) invasive adenocarcinoma of the lung; tumor cell degeneration, focal necrosis, hyperplasia of fibrous tissue, inflammatory cell infiltration, and histiocyte response observed in the lesions. The maximum diameter of the tumor was approximately 2 cm; no carcinoma was observed at the bronchial resection margin; tumor infiltration was observed at the lobar and segmental bronchi; visceral pleural invasion of the tumor was not seen; vascular infiltration was observed and definite nerve bundle infiltration was not found; (the second and the fourth groups of lymph nodes) no tumor metastases were found in the seven detected lymph nodes (0/7); (the seventh group of lymph nodes) tumor metastases were found in the 10 detected lymph nodes (2/10).
The patient was diagnosed with invasive adenocarcinoma of the right lung (stage pT1cN2M0 IIIA) at discharge, and the use of EGFR-TKI will be reinitiated based on patient recovery and relevant follow-up assessments.
Discussion
Aumolertinib and osimertinib are both orally administered third-generation irreversible EGFR-TKI that have demonstrated remarkable inhibitory activity against NSCLC cell lines harboring EGFR-sensitizing mutations and EGFR T790M resistance mutation [10,12,13]. These two medications provide long-term survival benefits to patients, but the consequent adverse reactions are also worthy of our attention.
Our case report suggested that in the course of neoadjuvant treatment with osimertinib for the patient with EGFR, TP53 mutation, and stage IIIA NSCLC, the patient developed myocardial damage with an elevated level of creatine kinase, which induced cardiac insufficiency, resulting in pulmonary arterial hypertension and pulmonary edema, as well as interstitial changes to both lungs. After osimertinib discontinuation and five days of symptomatic treatment, the patient experienced reduced pleural effusion and a decrease in the level of creatine kinase to normal values. After 46 days of treatment with aumolertinib following osimertinib discontinuation, interstitial edema in both lungs was absorbed, and the small amount of pleural effusion on both sides was also absorbed. The level of creatine phosphokinase rose to 227U/L, but the patient did not exhibit any relevant symptoms, and the level of CEA dropped to 3.79 ng/mL, which suggested good therapeutic effects.
This case report indicated that osimertinib-induced myocardial damage deserves our vigilant attention, and the induced myocardial damage may result in an elevated level of creatine kinase. However, in most studies on osimertinib (including studies by AURA2 [14], AURA3 [15] and FLAURA [16]), creatine kinase elevations were not statistically analyzed. We should also pay attention to other cardiotoxicities in administrating osimertinib. The US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Events Reporting System suggested an increased odds ratio for heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and QT interval prolongation due to osimertinib compared with other EGFR-TKIs [17]. Anad et al. [18]. also reported a higher incidence of osimertinib-induced cardiac AEs (6.1%) compared with other EGFR-TKIs (2.1%). In the FLAURA phase III registered clinical trial, the incidence of osimertinib-induced QT interval prolongation was 10%, and the incidence of QT interval prolongation ≥G3 was 2% [16], whereas in the AENEAS phase III registered trial on aumolertinib, the incidence of QT interval prolongation ≥G3 was 0.9% [13]. In this case report, after treatment with aumolertinib following discontinuation of osimertinib, the patient also experienced a slight increase in the level of creatine kinase, but did not present with other symptoms or diseases. In addition, cases of aumolertinib-induced myocardial damage have yet to be reported.
Although the underlying mechanism of osimertinib-related cardiotoxicity remains unclear, several case reports have suggested the development of cardiac dysfunction related to osimertinib treatment in some patients [17–19]. Cardiotoxicity can be divided into two types: reversible and irreversible cardiotoxicity. Irreversible cardiotoxicity is accompanied by myocardial damage, while reversible cardiotoxicity does not involve myocardial structural changes [20]. To date, it remains unclear whether osimertinib-induced cardiotoxicity is reversible. Oyakawa et al. [19]. described a case of osimertinib-induced myocarditis in which even after 12 weeks of discontinuation of osimertinib, there was no improvement in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). In contrast, the patient in this case report presented with reversible cardiotoxicity and cardiotoxicity did not occur after osimertinib was replaced by aumolertinib.
In addition, this patient developed interstitial changes in the lungs in the course of treatment with osimertinib, and after substitution with aumolertinib, interstitial changes did not occur. In the APOLLO trial on aumolertinib, the patients did not develop interstitial pneumonia of any grade [10], whereas in the AURA phase II [21], AURA2 [14], AURA 3 [15], and FLAURA [16] studies on osimertinib, the patients developed interstitial pneumonia. There are also reports of individual clinical cases who developed interstitial pneumonia after administration of osimertinib. After osimertinib was replaced by aumolertinib, interstitial pneumonia no longer occurred [22]. This is another factor that we considered in our decision to switch from osimertinib to aumolertinib for this patient.
Aumolertinib and osimertinib are both third-generation EGFR TKIs with differences in the chemical structural formula. Aumolertinib is structurally optimized by the introduction of cyclopropyl to the chemical structure of third-generation EGFR-TKIs, including aminopyrimidine parent nucleus + Michael addition receptor [12]. The introduction of cyclopropyl improves the metabolic stability of aumolertinib [23], resulting in less diversified metabolites than those of osimertinib. Aumolertinib and its metabolites demonstrate lower inhibitory activity against EGRF wild-type cells than osimertinib and its metabolites and can lower the incidence of AEs [24].
Surgery was successfully performed on this patient after administration of EGFR-targeting neoadjuvant therapy, which suggested the potential value of targeted drugs such as aumolertinib in the neoadjuvant treatment of EGFR-positive NSCLC. NSCLC patients need to have good cardiopulmonary functions before undergoing surgery, and preoperative pulmonary functional capacity is directly correlated with post-operative complications. Cardiopulmonary complications can affect postoperative rehabilitation and prognosis [25]. Hence, it is especially important to ensure the safety of medications for neoadjuvant therapy.
In summary, osimertinib-induced myocardial damage in NSCLC patients deserves our vigilant attention in clinical practice. Given the differences between aumolertinib and osimertinib in terms of chemical structure and cardiotoxicity data in clinical trials, if cardiotoxicity occurs after administration of osimertinib, a possible alternative option is to reinitiate treatment with aumolertinib after full recovery from cardiotoxicity; however, different cardiac markers need to be closely monitored. More clinical data are required to confirm the cardiac safety of aumolertinib. In this case, aumolertinib-induced serum CK elevation was not accompanied by clinical symptoms or abnormalities in other indicators, which is consistent with the clinical trial data on aumolertinib.
